title: Be slow to judge (Avot 1:1)
hook: the Great Assembly: be deliberate in judgment, raise many students, build a fence round the Torah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai, and it was handed down all the way to the Great Assembly. Today, that last link finally speaks. Day two hundred thirty-four.

It takes about a second. A screenshot, a headline, a neighbor's car parked badly, a coworker's short email. And the verdict is in. Guilty. Rude. Lazy. Clueless. People judge faster than they breathe, and the internet has made it a sport. Now picture a council of sages, the Great Assembly, at the end of that long chain from Sinai. They've been handed everything. And when Avot finally gives them a voice, the very first advice they pass on is about speed.
screen: `THE ONE-SECOND VERDICT.` → `GUILTY, RUDE, LAZY.` → `THE FIRST ADVICE IN AVOT.`

segments.voice: The men of the Great Assembly, Avot says, said three things. Be deliberate in judgment. Raise up many students. And make a fence around the Torah. The first one holds today's word. In Hebrew, hevu metunim ba-din. Metunim means slow, measured, patient: the slowness of someone who takes a second look. They were speaking first to judges, the people who decide real cases, and Jewish law built that slowness into its courts. The Mishnah says that in a capital case, the old high court could acquit a person on the same day, but could not convict on the same day. A guilty verdict had to wait until tomorrow, so the judges would sleep on it and look for any merit they'd missed. Mercy could be quick. Condemnation had to be slow. The other two sayings fit around this one. Raise up many students: don't hoard what you know. One old story says the school of Shammai wanted to teach only the worthy, and the school of Hillel said teach everyone. Make a fence around the Torah: a little margin of care, so you don't stumble over the line itself. But the order matters. Before students, before fences: slow down. Few people sit on a court, but everyone judges all day long. Kids, partners, strangers on a train. The sages' first advice: whatever verdict you're about to reach, let it wait a moment longer.
screen: `THREE THINGS FROM THE ASSEMBLY.` · `METUNIM — SLOW AND MEASURED.` · `ACQUIT TODAY, CONVICT TOMORROW.` · `STUDENTS AND A FENCE.` · then, large: `JUDGE SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Think of a verdict you reached recently, fast, about a coworker, a relative, a stranger, someone online, and put it on hold, like the old court. Ask what you might not know, and what a good lawyer for this person would say. You don't have to change your mind; just let the verdict wait until tomorrow.
Metunim. Measured, patient, slow to decide: the word behind the Great Assembly's first saying in Avot, be deliberate in judgment.
Your line: judge slowly. The sages put it first for a reason. Day two hundred thirty-four, done.

howItsDone: Jewish law sets out careful procedures for courts, including questioning witnesses closely and, in capital cases, delaying any guilty verdict until the next day, and Avot's call to judge deliberately is often applied to everyday life.
